Our mission To help every owner understand their pet better and teach it good habits, with clear, step-by-step explanations and no jargon. A relationship built on trust makes life easier for the animal and for the whole family. How we work Reward-based methods. We recommend positive reinforcement, clicker training, targeting, managing the environment and desensitisation: the approaches supported by animal behaviour research and veterinary associations. Never pain or fear. We advise against choke, prong and electric collars, physical punishment and “dominance” theory, which rest on outdated ideas and can harm an animal's welfare. Health first. t: Cat scratching the sofa: 6 solutions that work
d: Is your cat scratching the sofa? Why cats scratch, how to gently redirect them to a scratching post and which scratching post to choose.
h: Why cats scratch · 1. A scratching post more attractive than the sofa · 2. Put it in the right place · 3. Add a horizontal one · 4. Make it irresistible · 5. Make the sofa less appealing (temporarily) · 6. Look after its claws
x: Home › Tips › Cat scratching the sofa Cat scratching the sofa: 6 solutions that work 🐈 Cat · Beginner · 5 min read · Updated October 15, 2026 Your cat isn't scratching the sofa to annoy you. Scratching is a vital need. The goal isn't to stop it, but to offer a better place to do it. Why cats scratch To mark their territory : glands between the paw pads leave scent, and the marks are a visual message. To look after their claws by shedding the old outer sheaths. To stretch their whole body, often on waking. The sofa is perfect for all of this: stable, tall, well placed in the living room and full of your scent. 1. A scratching post more attractive than the sofa Instead of the sofa, offer a tall, stable post: the cat can stretch out fully on it. The ideal scratching post is stable (it mustn't wobble), tall enough for your cat to stretch out fully (at least 70-80 cm) and covered in a material it can shred, such as sisal. Small posts that tip over are often ignored. 🌳 A tall, stable scratching post A weighted sisal column, or a cat tree with a large post. See prices 2. Put it in the right place Place it right in front of the damaged part of the sofa , not in a hidden corner. Once the habit is formed, you can move it a few centimetres a day. Add another one near where your cat sleeps: cats scratch a lot when they wake up. 3. Add a horizontal one Some cats prefer to scratch flat surfaces (rugs, doormats). Watch yours: if it goes for the bottom of the sofa or the rug, add a cardboard scratcher on the floor. 📦 A cardboard scratcher Inexpensive and much loved by cats who scratch horizontally. See prices 4. Make it irresistible Rub some catnip on it, drag a feather wand around and over it so your cat sinks its claws in, and reward (treat, stroke) every time it uses it. That's positive reinforcement . 🌿 Catnip Many cats react to it, but not all: yours may well ignore it. See prices 5. Make the sofa less appealing (temporarily) For a few weeks, cover the scratched area with a throw or double-sided tape, which cats don't like touching. That's managing the environment : your cat stops reinforcing the habit in the wrong place while it learns the right one. 6. Look after its claws Regularly trimmed claws do less damage. Get your cat used to it gently with cooperative care : one claw a day, one treat each time. Never: shout at, spray or punish your cat. d: Yes, cats can be trained! Litter tray, scratching, coming when called, the carrier, handling and clicker tricks: every method for your cat.
h: 🪣 The litter tray · 💅 Scratching · 📣 Coming when called · 🧳 Loving the carrier · 🔘 Clicker training a cat · 🎣 Hunting, biting and energy
x: Home › Cat 🐈 Training your cat (yes, it's possible!) Cats learn very well… as long as you use rewards, very short sessions and plenty of patience. Punishment, on the other hand, doesn't work at all with them. The 3 golden rules with a cat: 1 to 3-minute sessions , very tasty rewards (wet food, lickable treats) and never any force . 🪣 The litter tray Rule of thumb: one tray per cat plus one, in quiet rooms. Away from food and water bowls. Cleaned every day; many cats prefer an open tray and fine, unscented litter. Sudden house-soiling = a visit to the vet (urinary infection, stress). 🛒 Unscented clumping litter · Large litter trays 💅 Scratching Instead of the sofa, offer a tall, stable post: the cat can stretch out fully on it. Scratching is a vital need (marking, claw care, stretching). You don't stop it, you redirect it: Place a tall, stable scratching post right in front of the damaged area. Make it attractive: catnip, play with a wand toy around it. Reward every scratch in the right place. Temporarily make the forbidden area less pleasant (a throw, double-sided tape). 🛒 Tall scratching post · Cat tree · Catnip · Full article 📣 Coming when called Pair a sound (its name, a treat packet rustle, a click) with a favourite treat. Call it when it is 1 metre away, reward. Repeat. Increase the distance, then call from another room. Very handy for finding a hiding cat or bringing it in at night. 🛒 Lickable treats (top reward) 🧳 Loving the carrier Leave the carrier open in the living room all the time, with a blanket. Drop treats in it at random: it becomes a pleasant place. Feed meals in it, then close the door for a few seconds. Lift it a few centimetres, then take short trips. 🛒 Top-opening carrier 🔘 Clicker training a cat The click marks the exact moment the pet touches the target; the treat follows. Cats love the clicker . Easy tricks to start with: Touch a target with the nose ( targeting ). Sit by capturing . Paw , high five , jump onto a stool . Choose a soft-sounding clicker: some cats are sensitive to noise. 🛒 Cat clicker kits 🎣 Hunting, biting and energy A cat that ambushes your ankles is often bored. Give it 2 hunting play sessions a day (10 min) with a feather wand, ending with a “prey” treat. Never play with your hands: it would learn they are prey. 🛒 Feather wands · Puzzle toys

h: 🍼 A puppy's first days · 🚽 House training · 🪑 Sit, down, stay · 📣 Recall · 🦮 Loose-lead walking · 🏠 Learning to be left alone · 🔊 Barking · 🦷 Puppy biting · 🛒 Recommended gear for training your dog
x: Home › Dog 🐕 Training your dog, step by step From the puppy who has just arrived to the adopted adult dog, here are the essential lessons, in the order to work on them. A puppy's first days House training Sit, down, stay Recall Loose-lead walking Being left alone Barking Puppy biting Recommended gear 🍼 A puppy's first days Give it a quiet corner with a bed or an open crate. Start socialisation straight away, gently. Respect its sleep: a puppy sleeps 16 to 20 hours a day. Training sessions of 2 to 3 minutes, several times a day. Sign up for puppy classes that use positive methods. 🚽 House training Take it out on waking, after every meal, every play session and every 2 hours. Always to the same spot; wait calmly. Praise and reward while it goes or right after, on the spot. An accident? Clean without scolding using an enzymatic cleaner (bleach attracts urine). 🛒 Enzymatic cleaner · Puppy crate · Full article 🪑 Sit, down, stay 1. Sit: treat above the head · 2. Down: treat towards the floor · 3. Stay: hand raised, one step back. Sit: by luring , treat above the head. Down: from the sit, lower the treat between its front paws, then towards the floor. Stay: work on the “3 Ds” separately: duration (1 s, then 3, then 10), distance (one step back), then distractions . Never increase them at the same time. 📣 Recall Choose a dedicated word (“Here!”) never used for anything unpleasant. At home: say the word, reward with a “jackpot” (several great treats). Outside, use a 10 m long line for safety. Don't only call it to end the walk: call, reward, release. As a back-up: a recall whistle , which carries further than your voice and always sounds the same. Full article . 🦮 Loose-lead walking Left: the lead is tight, so you stop. Right: the lead is loose, so you walk on and reward. Tight lead = we stop. Loose lead = we move on ( Premack ). Reward often when it is at your side. Change direction when it pulls: it learns to keep an eye on where you're going. Prefer a Y-shaped harness, which doesn't press on the throat, to a collar. 🛒 Y-shaped harness · 2 m lead · Full article 🏠 Learning to be left alone Start by leaving for a few seconds into another room. Build up the duration gradually, without big goodbyes or big hellos. Give it something to do: a frozen stuffed toy, a snuffle mat. A camera lets you check it stays relaxed. 🛒 Stuffable Kong-type toy · Snuffle mat · Pet camera Destruction, howling or house-soiling as soon as you leave can signal separation anxiety: talk to you

t: My puppy bites: what should I do?
d: Is your puppy nipping hands, feet and clothes? Why puppies bite, how to teach a soft mouth and which toys to offer.
h: Why puppies bite · 1. Teach it to soften its bite · 2. Always offer an alternative · 3. Respect its naps · 4. Channel its energy · 5. Protect the children
x: Home › Tips › Puppy biting My puppy bites: what should I do? 🐶 Puppy · Beginner · 5 min read · Updated October 15, 2026 Scratched hands, holey socks, children who are scared… Puppy biting is exhausting, but it's normal. With the right habits, it decreases noticeably within a few weeks. Why puppies bite They explore with their mouths , just as a baby touches everything with its hands. They are teething , roughly between 3 and 6 months: chewing brings relief. They play the way they did with their littermates. They are tired or over-excited : the most underestimated cause. 1. Teach it to soften its bite Between puppies, a little yelp stops the game when a bite is too hard. Do the same: as soon as teeth press down, stop moving, calmly withdraw your hand and stop all interaction for 10 to 20 seconds. Then resume the game. It learns that biting hard makes the human disappear. 2. Always offer an alternative Hands aren't toys: always offer a chew toy instead. Keep chew toys within reach at all times. As soon as your puppy targets your hands: offer a toy instead. When it chews the toy: praise. This is the principle of ignoring + rewarding the alternative . 🦷 Teething toys Vary the textures (soft rubber, rope, freezable toy) to soothe the gums. See prices 3. Respect its naps A puppy needs 16 to 20 hours of sleep a day. A puppy biting frantically at the end of the day is often an exhausted puppy. Settle it somewhere quiet in its own corner with a chew toy: it often falls asleep within minutes. 🧸 A Kong-type stuffable toy Filled with wet food and frozen, it keeps puppies busy, calms them and helps them fall asleep. See prices 4. Channel its energy Replace some hand games with sniffing games: hide kibble in a snuffle mat. Sniffing is mentally tiring and calming, much more than running. 🌾 A snuffle mat An easy way to offer a calm, sniffing-based activity every day. See prices 5. Protect the children Children run and shout, which excites the puppy. Teach them to become “a statue” if the puppy nips, and never leave them alone together. A safety gate helps separate spaces at lively moments. Avoid: tapping the muzzle, holding the mouth shut, pinning the puppy to the ground. These gestures are frightening, can damage your relationship and increase the risk of real bites later. If biting comes with stiff growling, a frozen body or continues after 6 months, ask your vet for advice. Key takeaways: stop the game when it presses too hard, offer a toy, respect nap time and channel

t: Dog pulling on the lead: how to make it stop
d: Does your dog pull on the lead on every walk? Why dogs pull, the “be a tree” method, changes of direction and the right harness to help.
h: Why dogs pull · The golden rule: tight lead = we stop · Reward the right position · Changes of direction · The right equipment · How long does it take?
x: Home › Tips › Dog pulling on the lead Dog pulling on the lead: how to make it stop 🐕 Dog · Beginner · 5 min read · Updated October 15, 2026 Aching arms, exhausting walks, a dog choking itself… Pulling on the lead is one of the most common problems. The good news: you can fix it without force, just with consistency. Why dogs pull Quite simply because it works : every time your dog pulls, it moves towards what it wants to sniff. Dogs also naturally walk faster than we do. It isn't trying to “dominate”: it has simply learnt that pulling is effective. The golden rule: tight lead = we stop Left: the lead is tight, so you stop. Right: the lead is loose, so you walk on and reward. This is the “be a tree” method. As soon as the lead goes tight, you freeze like a tree. You wait for your dog to release the tension (it turns round, takes a step back, sits). As soon as the lead is loose again: “Yes!” and off you go. It learns that a loose lead makes you move forward . It's a direct application of the Premack principle : moving towards what interests your dog becomes its reward. Reward the right position While walking, every time your dog is at your side with a loose lead, mark it (“Yes!” or a click ) and give a treat next to your leg . At first, reward every 2-3 steps, then space it out. 🦴 Training treats Small and soft, they're eaten in a second without breaking the rhythm of the walk. See prices Changes of direction If your dog charges ahead, turn round gently while cheerfully inviting it to follow you, then reward when it catches up. It learns to keep an eye on you, because you're unpredictable. The right equipment A Y-shaped harness leaves the throat free; a collar the dog pulls against presses on the neck. A collar that a dog pulls against presses on the windpipe and throat. A Y-shaped harness , which leaves the shoulders free, is far more comfortable and safer. Combined with a 2 m lead, it gives enough slack for your dog to walk without tension. 🦺 A Y-shaped harness Choose one that fits well (two fingers under the straps) and doesn't cross in front of the shoulders. See prices Choke, prong or shock collars stop pulling through pain. They cause injuries and fear, and don't teach your dog where to walk. Why we advise against them . How long does it take? The first progress shows within a few days if the whole family applies the same rule on every outing. d: Box clicker, button clicker, adjustable volume or target stick kit: which clicker to choose for your dog, cat, rabbit or bird, and how to get started.
h: Reminder: what is a clicker for? · The 4 types of clicker compared · 1. The classic “box” clicker · 2. The button clicker: the most versatile · 3. The adjustable-volume clicker: for sensitive animals · 4. The clicker + target stick kit · Which clicker for which pet? · Get started in 3 steps
x: Home › Tips › Clicker comparison Which clicker should you choose to train your pet? 🐕🐈 All species · Buying guide · 5 min read · Updated October 16, 2026 The clicker is one of the cheapest and most effective training tools. But they're not all the same: a sound that's too loud can scare a cat, a stiff button tires your hand. Here's how to choose yours. In short: for a dog, a button clicker with a wrist strap works very well. For a cat, a rabbit or a fearful animal, choose a soft-sounding or adjustable-volume clicker . For birds and targeting, a clicker + target stick kit is the most practical. Reminder: what is a clicker for? The click marks the exact moment the pet touches the target; the treat follows. The click is a “marker”: it tells the animal the exact moment it does the right thing, and announces a reward. Its strength is its precision and consistency: the sound is always the same, unlike your voice. The whole method is explained in our guide to clicker training . The 4 types of clicker compared Type Sound Strengths Best for Classic “box” clicker Loud, sharp Easy to hear outdoors, very cheap Dogs not bothered by noise, outdoor work Button clicker Medium Ergonomic, easy to press, often with a strap Most dogs, beginners Adjustable-volume clicker Adjustable Adapts to sensitive animals Cats, rabbits, fearful dogs Clicker + target stick Varies Two tools in one, ideal for targeting Birds, cats, rabbits, agility tricks 1. The classic “box” clicker This is the original model: a small box with a metal tongue. Its loud click carries well outdoors. On the other hand, it can make sensitive animals jump. If so, start by holding it away from you or muffling it in a pocket. 2. The button clicker: the most versatile The button is easy to press with one finger without looking, which helps you click at the right moment. The sound is a little softer than the classic box. The i-Click, designed by the team of Karen Pryor, one of the pioneers of clicker training, is a well-known model of this type. 🔘 Button clicker with wrist strap The strap or wristband saves you hunting for it mid-session. See prices 👆 i-Click A button clicker with a fairly soft sound, designed for clicker training. See prices 3. The adjustable-volume clicker: for sensitive animals Some models offer several sound levels. It's the right choice for a cat, a rabbit, a small rodent or a fearful dog: start at the lowest volume, then turn it up if needed for outdoor work. 🔉 Adjustable-volume clicker To start

x: Home › Tips › Scratching post comparison Which scratching post should you choose for your cat? Our comparison 🐈 Cat · Buying guide · 6 min read · Updated October 16, 2026 Plenty of scratching posts end up ignored in a corner while the cat carries on attacking the sofa. The problem rarely lies with the cat: it's usually the post that doesn't suit it. Here's how to choose one your cat will really use. In short: for a first scratching post, choose a tall (at least 70–80 cm), heavy and stable sisal post , and add a flat cardboard scratcher if your cat scratches rugs. The 4 criteria that really matter Instead of the sofa, offer a tall, stable post: the cat can stretch out fully on it. Stability. A post that wobbles or tips over scares the cat, who won't come back. This is the number one criterion. Height. Your cat must be able to stretch out fully, front legs extended: allow at least 70 to 80 cm for an adult cat. Material. Woven sisal (rope or fabric) is the favourite. Cardboard is very popular for scratching flat. Carpet is less advisable: it looks just like your rugs. Direction. Some cats scratch vertically (sofa, doors), others horizontally (rugs, doormats). Watch yours before you buy. Our comparison 🐕 Dog · Buying guide · 7 min read · Updated October 16, 2026 A good harness protects your dog's neck, makes walks more pleasant and helps with loose-lead training. But between Y-front, no-pull, H-shaped and “Norwegian” harnesses, it's hard to know where to start. Here's our comparison to help you choose. In short: for most dogs, a Y-front harness with two rings (one on the back, one on the chest) is the best choice: it leaves the shoulders free and helps your dog learn not to pull. Why a harness rather than a collar? A Y-shaped harness leaves the throat free; a collar the dog pulls against presses on the neck. When a dog pulls on a collar, all the pressure goes on the throat and neck, a delicate area (windpipe, thyroid, neck vertebrae). A harness spreads that pressure across the chest. This matters most for dogs that still pull, small dogs, flat-faced breeds and dogs with breathing problems. A collar is still useful for carrying the ID tag. The Y-front harness: the best everyday choice Seen from the front, its straps form a “Y” that runs between the front legs and clears the shoulders. Your dog keeps a natural stride, which makes it ideal for long walks, canicross or hiking. 🦺 Y-front harness Look for straps that adjust in at least 4 places and padding on the chest. See prices 2. The two-clip harness: for learning not to pull This is a Y-front harness with a second ring on the chest. With the lead clipped at the front, a dog that pulls is gently turned back towards you instead of moving forwards: a real help while you work on loose-lead walking , without any pain. The Ruffwear Front Range is a well-known model of this type; many other brands make an equivalent. 🔁 Y-front harness with chest ring The most versatile: front clip for training, back clip afterwards. Pet: All 🐕 Dog 🐈 Cat 🐇 Rabbit/rodent 🦜 Bird Level: All Beginner Intermediate Advanced List of methods Beginner All species ⭐ Positive reinforcement The core principle: a behaviour followed by something pleasant (a treat, play, a stroke) is more likely to happen again. It is the basis of almost every other method. How to use it Pick a reward your pet truly loves (not necessarily its everyday kibble). Reward within 1 to 2 seconds of the right behaviour. Keep sessions short (3 to 5 min) in a quiet place. Increase difficulty gradually: distance, duration, then distractions. Once learnt, space out food rewards and vary them (play, praise). 🛒 Useful: training treats · treat pouch Beginner All species 🔘 Clicker training The click is a “marker”: it tells your pet the precise moment it did the right thing, and a reward follows. Used with dolphins, horses, dogs, cats and even fish. How to use it Charge the clicker: click → treat, 10 to 15 times, without asking for anything. Check: when you click, your pet turns its head towards you expecting a reward. Click only at the exact moment of the right behaviour, then reward. One click = always one reward, even if you clicked too early. Add a verbal cue only once the behaviour is reliable. Tip: a short, consistent word (“Yes!”, “Good!”) can replace the clicker. 🛒 Useful: clicker with wrist strap · clicker training books Beginner Dog · Cat · Rabbit 🍖 Luring The treat guides the head up, the bottom goes down… and there's the sit! You guide your pet with a treat held near its nose to bring it into a position. Very fast for teaching “sit”, “down” or “spin”. Example: teaching “sit” Treat in front of the nose, slowly raise your hand above its head. The head goes up, the bottom goes down: mark and reward as soon as it touches the floor. After 5 successes, make the same gesture without a treat in that hand, and reward with the other hand. The gesture becomes a hand signal; then add the word “sit”. ⚠️ Fade the lure quickly, or your pet will only respond when it sees food. Reward-based methods, and targeting in particular, give amazing results. 🐇 Rabbits Hay in the tray helps rabbits learn to use it; a gently offered leaf helps them build trust. Litter training Rabbits naturally go in one corner. Put a litter tray there (plant-based litter, never clumping cat litter) with hay next to it: they eat and toilet at the same time. 🛒 Plant-based litter · Tray with hay rack Trust and handling Never pick a rabbit up by the ears and avoid lifting it by surprise. Get down on the floor, let it come to you, offer a blade of grass or a piece of vegetable. Being carried is learnt very gradually ( cooperative care ). Clicker and agility Rabbits can learn to come to their name, touch a target, jump small hurdles or go into their pen. Reward: small pieces of vegetables or fresh herbs. 🛒 Agility set · Indoor pen 🐀 Rats, mice and ferrets Rats quickly learn to touch a target; ferrets let off steam on a toy rather than your hands. Rats: brilliant students Very intelligent, rats learn their name, recall, pushing levers or running courses. Stick targeting works wonderfully. Reward: a tiny piece of cereal or fruit. 🛒 Enrichment toys Ferrets: stopping the nipping Ferrets play by nipping. If one bites too hard, stop the game and calmly put it down for a few seconds ( extinction ). Reward gentle play. Ferrets can also learn to use a litter tray and wear a harness. 🛒 Ferret harness 🦜 Birds Hand held just above the feet, under the belly: the bird learns to step up on its own. Budgies, cockatiels and parrots are brilliant students. Targeting and the clicker are the basic tools of zoo keepers. Stepping up onto the hand Offer a treat (a millet spray) near the cage, without going in. Then your open hand inside the cage, keeping still. Place a finger or perch just above the feet, in front of the belly. As soon as one foot steps on: reward. Add the word “step up”. Targeting for birds Teach your bird to touch the tip of a stick with its beak. You can then guide it to the cage, the scales or a perch without ever grabbing it. 🛒 Bird clicker + target kit Talking and screaming For talking, use the model/rival method . For screaming, don't come running in response (that reinforces it): reward calm moments and soft sounds. 🛒 Play stands · Foraging toys Wing clipping and forced handling damage trust. h: Why your puppy isn't house-trained yet · 1. Go out at the right times · 2. Always the same spot · 3. Reward at the right moment · 4. Supervise or limit the space · 5. Clean up accidents properly · 6. What about at night? · What about puppy pads?
x: Home › Tips › House training a puppy House training your puppy: the method that works 🐶 Puppy · Beginner · 6 min read · Updated October 15, 2026 Puddles in the living room, rugs to wash, night-time wake-ups… House training is often the first challenge with a puppy. The good news: with routine and patience, most puppies are house-trained within a few weeks to a few months. Why your puppy isn't house-trained yet A young puppy doesn't yet have good bladder control . It needs to go often, and it doesn't yet know that the house isn't the right place: at the breeder's, it often went wherever it happened to be. So it never does it “on purpose” or “out of spite”. Your job is to show it where to go, at the right time, and to make that place very rewarding. 1. Go out at the right times On waking, after meals, after play and before bed: outside you go… then a reward! The secret is to anticipate: take your puppy out before it has a chance to get it wrong. The key moments: on waking, in the morning and after every nap; after every meal (within 15 to 30 minutes); after a play session or excitement; before bed in the evening; and, on top of that, at regular intervals during the day (every 1 to 2 hours at first). Watch for the signs too: sniffing the floor while circling, heading for the door, suddenly wandering off. If so, go out immediately. 2. Always the same spot Always take your puppy to the same patch of grass, on the lead, and wait calmly without playing. The smell of its previous visits will encourage it to go there again. You can say a gentle, consistent word (“busy”) while it goes: over time, it will link it to the action. 3. Reward at the right moment This is the heart of the method, based on positive reinforcement : as soon as it has finished, on the spot , praise enthusiastically and give a treat. If you wait until you're back inside, it won't make the connection. Keep rewards on you so you never miss that moment. 🦴 Training treats Small and very tasty, keep them in your pocket on every outing to reward within a second. See prices 4. Supervise or limit the space A puppy wandering alone around the whole house will inevitably have accidents out of sight. When you can't supervise it, limit its space to one room or a pen with its bed: dogs generally avoid soiling where they sleep. d: Your dog won't come back when called? The 7-step method for a reliable recall, even at the park, with the mistakes to avoid and the gear that helps.

x: Home › Tips › Dog recall How to teach your dog a reliable recall in 7 steps 🐕 Dog · Beginner · 6 min read · Updated October 15, 2026 A dog who comes back when called means more freedom for them and less stress for you. Recall isn't about having a “good” or “bad” dog: it's a skill, built step by step. Why your dog doesn't come back In your dog's mind, the question is simple: what's in it for me? If the smell in the grass, the dog friend or the squirrel is more interesting than you, the smell wins. And if your dog has been told off for coming back, or if every recall means “the walk is over”, it has actually learnt not to come back. The solution: make coming back the best deal of its day , using positive reinforcement . Step 1: choose a “fresh” cue If “Come!” has already been shouted a hundred times with no result, it no longer means anything. Choose a new word (“Here!”, “Touch!”) or a whistle blast, and use it only for recall. 📣 A recall whistle It sounds the same whatever your mood, and carries much further than your voice. See prices Step 2: “charge” the cue at home In the living room, with no distractions, say your word and immediately give an outstanding reward: a piece of chicken, cheese, a treat it never gets otherwise. Repeat 10 times a day for 3 days. Your dog doesn't even need to move: it is learning that this word announces something amazing. Step 3: first real recalls at short distance When it is 2 metres away and slightly distracted, say the word. As soon as it arrives: party and reward. Gradually increase the distance, then call it from another room. Step 4: go outside… with a long line With a long line, your dog enjoys its freedom and learns that coming back to you is always a party. Outside, distractions explode. A long line (a 10 m lead) lets you give your dog freedom while preventing it from learning that it can ignore the recall. Never use it to reel your dog in: it is only there to stop it leaving. ➰ A 10 m long line Choose a biothane line: it doesn't soak up water and is easy to clean. Use it with a harness, never a collar. See prices Step 5: the “jackpot” When it comes back in a difficult situation (it was playing with another dog), give a jackpot : several treats in a row, a game with its favourite toy. It will remember that it was really worth it. 👝 A treat pouch So rewards are within reach at the right moment, without rummaging in your pockets.
